newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat rejects Netanyahu plea to change deal.
newsitem.headline: Arafat rejects Netanyahu plea to change deal.

text.p: PLO officials said on Monday that U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross had yet to bridge wide gaps between Israel and the Palestinians on implementation of a long- delayed Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

They said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat rejected a proposal by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that they could hold a summit on Monday if Arafat agreed to change the Hebron deal signed a year ago by Israel's previous government and give Israel powers in areas that were to be given the PLO.

Netanyahu, facing rancour in the Arab world focused on delays on implementing deals with the PLO among other things, dispatched President Ezer Weizman to Egypt on Monday in a bid to mend a deep rift at the heart of the Middle East conflict.

The outspoken Weizman, whose office is largely ceremonial, said his role in Egypt would be to seek to heal "certain splits, which everyone sees, with the largest Arab country, and I think we can find a number of directions for improved relations".

Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters on Monday: "The (Israeli) aim in the security and civilian committees is to try to change the agreements. They want powers in H1. This is impossible. President Arafat's instructions are not to reopen the agreement."
"H1" is the area to be handed to Palestinian rule in Hebron under the signed deal.

A PLO official speaking on condition he not be named said Arafat, in the West Bank town of Nablus, had rejected the Netanyahu proposal brought by Ross on Sunday night. Arafat left Nablus on Monday morning for Jericho. He was to go later in the day to Jordan to meet with King Hussein.
Palestinian officials say changes Israel is demanding include control of ridges in the town that were to be Palestinian and to retain zoning and planning authority.
The ridges overlook the area of Hebron where most of some 400 Jewish settlers living amidst 100,000 Palestinians stay in fortified enclaves.
Efforts continue to bridge gaps but Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah said that contacts on arranging an Arafat-Netanyahu summit had stopped.
Palestinian officials said they expected Ross would meet Netanyahu on Monday. Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak told Reuters such a meeting was always possible but none had been set.
The sides on Sunday delayed for at least one day formal talks on Hebron, set to reconvene on Monday in the Egyptian resort of Taba to see if other channels might bear fruit.
Arafat and Netanyahu last met early this month at an emergency summit in Washington after fierce Palestinian-Israeli clashes last month in which 60 Arabs and 15 Jews were killed.
The fighting threatened to scuttle the 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal, and sparked fears of a return to Arab-Israeli warfare.
Israel's ties with its Arab neighbours, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and the Palestinians, all but ruptured after Netanyahu's upset victory over Shimon Peres in May elections.
Netanyahu put Arabs on notice that Peres's U.S.-endorsed formula of trading occupied land for peace, the formula that guided Israel's previous government, was not his policy.

Though Netanyahu has pledged to honour commitments sealed by Nobel Peace laureates Rabin and Peres, his failure thus far to order the Hebron redeployment has taken centre stage in Arab eyes as a test of the tough-talking Israeli leader's intentions.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has said the Hebron issue must be settled before he will agree to meet Netanyahu.
